notes.b: A purchase involves several parties, and each has a different relationship to the consumer. Knowing who is who tells you where to go when something goes wrong.
points: The consumer is an individual who buys goods or services for personal use, not for business, so a shopper buying a kettle for the kitchen is a consumer.
The retailer or trader sells goods or services in the course of business and is the consumer's first point of contact for a complaint, because the consumer's contract is with the seller.
Under consumer law the retailer is responsible for faults in goods, even when the manufacturer made the fault, and must deal with the complaint.
The manufacturer makes the product and is the other party to any manufacturer's guarantee (a written promise to repair or replace a faulty product).
A guarantee is a contract between the manufacturer and the consumer. It is usually offered in addition to the consumer's statutory rights (rights set by law), not instead of them.
The supplier or distributor moves goods from the manufacturer to the retailer, so the consumer rarely deals with this party directly.
notes.tip: A common sentence-completion asks what a guarantee is: a contract between the manufacturer and the consumer. Remember that a guarantee adds to statutory rights and never replaces them, and that the retailer, not the manufacturer, is the first point of contact for those rights.

notes.b: Informed decisions rest on reliable information. It comes from the product itself, from the seller and from independent sources, and each should be checked against the others.
points: Labels, instructions and care labels give the contents or ingredients, how to use and care for the product, and warnings about hazards, so they should be read before buying and using.
Unit pricing shows the price per kilogram or per litre, which allows comparison between different pack sizes.
Advertising and sales material is useful but should be checked against the product label and independent information, because the seller wants to make the sale.
Independent consumer publications and testing reports compare products on quality and value for money. The Consumers' Association of Ireland publishes comparative findings in Consumer Choice.
Citizens Information gives free, confidential information on consumer rights, so a consumer can ask about a problem without cost.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission publishes guidance on consumer rights and on unfair trading.
Terms and conditions, the returns policy and guarantee wording should be read before purchase, as they set out what the seller offers.

Marks and symbols are information too: quality marks such as the Bord Bia Quality Mark, the CE mark (the manufacturer declares the product meets EU safety requirements), the energy rating label on appliances, and safety and hazard symbols.
Reviews, word of mouth and online comparison sites are useful but may be biased, so check more than one source.
notes.tip: If asked to name a reliable source of consumer advice, give Citizens Information or the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission.

notes.b: A consumer's part in a transaction is to be informed, careful and honest. These are the consumer's duties, which are different from the rights the consumer is entitled to.
points: Know your rights and the laws that protect consumers: the basic rights and remedies under consumer law apply whether or not the seller mentions them.
Be informed about goods and services before buying, and compare value, not only price, by weighing price against quality, durability and the cost of running or maintaining the product.
Read and understand labels and terms before buying, including ingredients, dates, guarantee conditions and cancellation terms.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions and care labels; a fault caused by misuse is unlikely to be the trader's responsibility.
Keep receipts and proof of purchase, since they show when, where and what was bought, and are needed for a claim.
notes.tip: Examiners accept answers such as be informed and know your rights, read labels, follow instructions, keep receipts, complain where appropriate, judge quality against price, use resources responsibly and give accurate information when complaining. Keep responsibilities (duties) separate from rights (entitlements).

notes.h: Acting on problems and planning purchases
notes.b: The consumer's duties continue after the sale. A responsible consumer also acts quickly when something goes wrong and plans spending so that problems are less likely.
points: Report faults promptly, stop using a faulty or unsafe product, and complain where appropriate, as delay can make a problem harder to prove.
Give accurate, truthful information when complaining, including a clear description of the problem and the redress (the remedy) wanted.
Plan purchases and set a budget: check whether a product is needed before buying.
Resist pressure selling and impulse buying, and do not be rushed by sales talk, because a quick decision leaves no time to compare or check.
Check the total cost, including interest and charges, before agreeing to credit or easy-pay arrangements, because the instalments can add up to far more than the cash price.
Use resources responsibly and consider the environment: reduce waste, and reuse and recycle packaging.
notes.tip: For a question on how responsibilities help wise choices, link each duty to its result. Reading labels avoids unsuitable or unsafe purchases (for example an allergen or a short guarantee); keeping receipts makes a refund possible; comparing value matters because a cheaper item that wears out quickly costs more over time; following instructions prevents damage that would leave you without a remedy; complaining with accurate details gets the problem put right and helps other consumers; budgeting reduces impulse buying and debt. In scenario questions, say which responsibilities the shopper should have shown.

notes.b: Traditional buying principles still shape how a consumer should approach a purchase, even though the law now gives buyers more protection.
points: Caveat emptor is a Latin principle meaning 'let the buyer beware': it places the duty of checking goods on the buyer, so the buyer had to inspect goods before buying.
Modern consumer law limits caveat emptor by giving statutory rights that apply automatically, but inspecting goods and asking questions before purchase remains the best protection.
A needs-based decision is guided by necessity and income; a wants-based decision is more open to advertising and impulse buying.
Vague claims such as 'the best' or 'new' that lack supporting evidence should be questioned before they influence a purchase, because they sound impressive but promise nothing that can be checked.

notes.b: Consumer rights are what a buyer is entitled to expect. Papers list them in slightly different ways, so learn the rights below as the common set.
points: Right to safety: goods and services must not endanger health or life.
Right to honest and truthful information about goods and services, so that buyers can decide on accurate facts.
Right to choice: a range of goods and services is available to choose from.
Right to value for money: goods and services should be of a quality that matches the price paid, and goods should be of satisfactory quality.
Right to redress: a consumer whose goods or service are faulty can seek repair, replacement or a refund.
Right to services completed to a high standard, by a qualified person, using good materials.
There is no right to a refund simply for a change of mind in a shop purchase; a retailer may offer an exchange or a credit note as goodwill.
Rights and responsibilities are linked: each right is only as useful as the consumer's knowledge and action, so a right to information works only if labels are read.
notes.tip: Name the right and explain it in one sentence. Do not present a fixed number of rights, since papers list between five and seven. In refund scenarios, a faulty camera means yes with proof of purchase, while a disliked colour means no statutory right.

keyTerms.definition: An individual who buys goods or services for personal use rather than for business purposes.
A business that sells goods or services to consumers and is their first point of contact for a complaint.
The business that makes a product and, where it gives one, provides the manufacturer's guarantee.
A contract between the manufacturer and the consumer, usually offered in addition to statutory rights.
A Latin principle meaning let the buyer beware, placing the duty to check goods on the buyer.
Evidence, such as a receipt, that shows when, where and what was bought.
The price per standard measure, such as per kilogram or per litre, used to compare pack sizes.
The remedy a consumer receives for a faulty product or service, such as repair, replacement or refund.

factCards.term: Three steps an informed consumer takes before buying
factCards.definition: Read the labels and terms, compare value and unit prices, and check whether the product is needed and what it will cost in total.

factCards.term: Latin principle that places the duty of checking goods on the buyer
factCards.definition: Caveat emptor, meaning let the buyer beware.

factCards.term: Consumer rights named in the marking schemes
factCards.definition: Right to safety, right to honest and truthful information, right to choice, right to value for money, right to quality, right to redress, and right to services done to a high standard.

factCards.term: Two things a consumer should keep to support a complaint
factCards.definition: The receipt or proof of purchase, and a record of when and where the goods were bought.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways in which a consumer can make an informed choice using the information available to them.
questions.model: Two ways, each explained with its purpose. Reading labels: ingredients, dates, nutrition information, care instructions and warnings allow the consumer to judge suitability, safety and use before buying. Comparing unit prices and quality: the price per kilogram or litre and the product's quality and durability show whether the purchase is good value. Other acceptable answers include checking advertising claims against independent information, reading terms and conditions, and seeking advice from Citizens Information.

questions.prompt: Discuss the responsibilities a consumer has in relation to information and rights when buying goods and services.
questions.model: Knowing rights: the consumer should understand the basic rights and remedies, which apply whether or not the seller mentions them. Reading information: labels, instructions, terms, guarantee conditions and cancellation terms should be read and understood before buying. Comparing value: price should be weighed against quality, durability and running costs, using unit prices where available. Records: receipts and proof of purchase must be kept, since they are needed for any claim. Using products properly: instructions and care labels should be followed, because misuse may defeat a claim. Reporting promptly: faults should be raised quickly and accurately, with a clear description of the redress wanted. Critical buying: vague advertising claims should be questioned, purchases planned, and the total cost of credit checked. A complete answer links each responsibility to the protection it gives the consumer.
